Chords

One chord, several ways to play it.

Choose a root to see all its chords. Compare open, barre and compact shapes, then use a position that suits the song and your hand.

Try it on the fretboard ↗

Understand

A major chord uses 1–3–5; minor lowers the third. A seventh adds another note. Sus2 and sus4 replace the third; add9 keeps the third and adds a second an octave above in the formula. Voicings can reorder those notes.

Standard tuning: E A D G B E, from the thickest string to the thinnest.

Root note

Root note: G

Fingers: 1 index · 2 middle · 3 ring · 4 little. O = open string; × = do not play. A thick line joins the strings held by one finger.

Make the connection

A chord name specifies a set of notes, not a single grip. G is G B D; G7 adds F, while Gmaj7 adds F♯. Gm changes B to B♭. A movable closed shape transposes when all frets move equally. Open strings must be moved or muted too; sliding only the fretted fingers is not a reliable transposition.

Play it

For G major, compare the two open fingerings with the E shape at fret 3 and the A shape at fret 10. Play each string separately before strumming only the strings marked O or with a dot.

These fixed tabs remain a G example when you change the explorer. Guitar compares an open G with the fret-3 barre. Ukulele compares two G voicings. Bass outlines G in bar 1, then adds F in bar 2 to suggest G7. Read all sounded strings before playing.

Six lines, from top to bottom: e B G D A E. String 1 is the thin E. The examples use standard tuning without a capo. Move the hand when needed instead of forcing a wide stretch.

A worked example

Read left to right. Counts above mark the beats; numbers on the lines are frets; numbers below give the duration in beats. R = rest. Stacked fret numbers sound together. Start at 60 BPM.

A mistake to avoid

A × above a chord diagram means skip that string; x on a tab usually means strike a muted note. Neither is a silent rest. A slash chord names its bass note: G/B keeps G B D with B lowest.

Listen and check

Use the least pressure that produces a clear sound. For a barre, bring the index finger close behind the fret. If a note buzzes, adjust that finger rather than squeezing the whole hand.

Ready for the next step?

Play a selected shape string by string without unwanted notes. Change to another voicing without losing four steady beats, even if you need a slower tempo.
